mainTopic: Who is exempt from ראיה and הקהל, and the אגדות and דרשות on הקהל that follow
overview: This amud opens with the end of a ברייתא. Someone who can speak but not hear, or hear but not speak, is פטור from ראיה but חייב in שמחה. Someone who can do neither, a שוטה, and a קטן are פטור even from שמחה. The גמרא explains that ראיה is linked to הקהל by a גזירה שוה. At הקהל, 'למען ישמעו' leaves out the deaf, and 'ולמען ילמדו', read as 'so they may teach', leaves out the mute, since a story shows that mute people can learn. רבי תנחום then rules that someone deaf in one ear, or lame in one leg, is exempt from ראיה, and the גמרא shows which word in the פסוק teaches each law. This leads to a few אגדות: רבא on the beautiful feet of ישראל going up for the רגל, and רבי תנחום on יוסף's pit full of snakes and scorpions. Finally, a ברייתא tells how רבי יהושע heard רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's דרשות on הקהל: little children come so their parents earn reward, and ישראל and ה׳ each make the other unique. The proof-פסוק for that last idea comes on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: who is exempt even from rejoicing
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes: a person who speaks but cannot hear, or hears but cannot speak, is still obligated in שמחה. But one who neither hears nor speaks, a שוטה, and a קטן are exempt even from שמחה, because they are exempt from all מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Such a person] is obligated in rejoicing. But one who neither hears nor speaks, a שוטה, and a minor are exempt even from rejoicing, since they are exempt from all the מצוות in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: We are hearing the last part of a ברייתא that started just before this section. It sorts people into who is exempt from what.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two groups appear here. The first is a person who only lacks hearing OR only lacks speech: he is פטור from ראיה but still חייב in שמחה. The second is a person who lacks both, a שוטה, or a קטן: they are פטור from everything, שמחה included, because they are outside all מצוות altogether.

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה to rejoice on the festival, by eating שלמי שמחה
The מצוה to appear in the בית המקדש on the festival, with an offering
A person who lacks mental competence
A minor, not yet obligated in מצוות

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two groups. Someone who lacks only hearing, or only speech, IS obligated in שמחה. Only someone who lacks both hearing and speech, a שוטה, or a קטן is exempt from שמחה.

phrases.english: is obligated in rejoicing.
phrases.notes: This finishes a ברייתא from just before, about someone who can hear but not speak, or speak but not hear.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶת שֶׁאֵינוֹ לֹא שׁוֹמֵעַ וְלֹא מְדַבֵּר,
phrases.english: And one who neither hears nor speaks,
and an imbecile and a minor —
are exempt even from rejoicing,
since they are exempt from all the מצוות
stated in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא that began before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, is obligated in שמחה. One who neither hears nor speaks, a שוטה, and a קטן are exempt even from שמחה, since they are exempt from all מצוות.

steps.title: Why exempt from appearing but obligated in rejoicing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a deaf person or a mute is exempt from ראיה but obligated in שמחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about appearing, that they are exempt, and what is different about rejoicing, that they are obligated?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's different treatment of the two מצוות. This sets up the next step, which gives the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ראיה and שמחה are festival מצוות, so we would expect the same people to be included in both. The גמרא wants to know what source makes ראיה different.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asking for the reason behind a distinction)

phrases.english: What is different regarding appearing, that they are exempt,
and what is different regarding rejoicing, that they are obligated?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the distinction made in the ברייתא
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that exempts a deaf person or a mute from ראיה but not from שמחה

steps.title: A word-link to הקהל explains the exemption from appearing
steps.stepSummary: ראיה is learned from הקהל through a גזירה שוה on the word 'ראיה', so whoever is exempt from הקהל is also exempt from ראיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Regarding appearing, we learn 'appearing' 'appearing' from הקהל. It says there: 'Assemble the people, the men, women and children,' and it also says: 'When all Israel comes to appear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ראיה has its own special source. It is connected to the מצוה of הקהל by a shared word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לראות' (to appear) is used about הקהל and also about the festival ראיה. That shared word creates a גזירה שוה linking the two, so the exemptions of הקהל carry over to ראיה. שמחה has no such link, so it keeps its broad obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: He derives, he learns (from another source)
The gathering of all Israel in the בית המקדש on סוכות after שמיטה to hear the תורה read
Learning one law from another because the same word appears in both

steps.whyThisMatters: This links the rules of ראיה to the rules of הקהל, which explains why the two מצוות are treated differently.

phrases.english: Regarding appearing, he derives
'appearing' 'appearing' from the assembly,
phrases.notes: The same word shows up in both places, so the laws are linked. That is a גזירה שוה.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'Assemble the people,
the men and the women and the little ones,'
phrases.notes: דברים 31:12

phrases.english: and it is written: 'When all Israel comes to appear.'
phrases.notes: דברים 31:11

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ראיה is linked to הקהל by a גזירה שוה, so whoever is exempt from הקהל is exempt from ראיה. שמחה has no such link.

steps.title: How do we know they are exempt from הקהל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that a deaf person or a mute is exempt from הקהל itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And there, by הקהל, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The previous answer depends on these people being exempt from הקהל. Now the גמרא asks how we know that. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גזירה שוה only moves the exemption over from הקהל. It does not prove the exemption exists at הקהל in the first place. So the גמרא needs a source for the original exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: And there (in the other case being referred to)
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: And there, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: 'There' means הקהל. How do we know a deaf person or a mute is exempt from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Digs one level deeper into the source used in step 3
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for exempting a deaf person or a mute from הקהל

steps.title: 'So that they may hear and so that they may learn'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains the פסוק: 'that they may hear' excludes one who cannot hear, and 'that they may learn' excludes one who cannot speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'So that they may hear and so that they may learn.' A ברייתא teaches: 'So that they may hear' leaves out one who speaks but does not hear. 'So that they may learn' leaves out one who hears but does not speak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the הקהל exemption. It comes from a ברייתא that reads the two halves of the פסוק as two separate exclusions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hearing is needed to take in the reading at הקהל, so a deaf person is left out. The ברייתא assumes that learning requires speaking, so a mute is left out too. That assumption is exactly what the next step questions.
steps.whatToRemember: The chain of sources is: ראיה is linked to הקהל by a גזירה שוה. At הקהל, 'ישמעו' excludes a deaf person and 'ילמדו' excludes a mute.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'So that they may hear
and so that they may learn,'
phrases.notes: דברים 31:12

phrases.english: and it was taught: 'So that they may hear' —
excludes one who speaks but does not hear;
'and so that they may learn' —
excludes one who hears but does not speak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'למען ישמעו ולמען ילמדו', as explained in a ברייתא: the first phrase excludes the deaf, the second excludes the mute.

steps.title: Can't a mute person learn? The story of two mutes in רבי's בית מדרש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that one who cannot speak cannot learn. It begins a story about two mute relatives of רבי יוחנן בן גודגדא who sat in רבי's study hall, nodding and moving their lips.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does that mean that one who cannot speak cannot learn? But there were two mute people in רבי's neighborhood, grandsons (some say nephews) of רבי יוחנן בן גודגדא. Whenever רבי entered the בית מדרש, they would come in and sit before the Sages, nodding their heads and moving their lips.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's assumption that a mute cannot learn. It starts a story to show that mutes seem able to follow learning, and the story finishes in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used 'ילמדו' to exclude a mute, which assumes that not speaking means not learning. The story describes two mutes who appeared to understand: they nodded and moved their lips along with the learning. The end of the story, in Step 7, proves that they really did learn, which completes the challenge. מר זוטרא answers it in Step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introducing a challenge to what was implied)

phrases.aramaic: לְמֵימְרָא דְּכִי לָא מִשְׁתַּעֵי לָא גָּמַר?
phrases.english: Is that to say that when one does not speak, he does not learn?
But there were those two mute people
who lived in Rebbi's neighborhood,
phrases.notes: רבי here is רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי בְרַתֵּיה דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן גּוּדְגְּדָא,
phrases.english: sons of the daughter of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּנֵי אֲחָתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: and some say, sons of the sister of Rabbi Yochanan,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכׇל אֵימַת דַּהֲוָה עָיֵיל רַבִּי לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
phrases.english: that whenever Rebbi would enter the study hall
they would enter and sit before them,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the Sages in the study hall.

phrases.english: and nod their heads and move their lips,

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּכִי לָא מִשְׁתַּעֵי לָא גָּמַר? וְהָא הָנְהוּ תְּרֵי אִילְּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind the ברייתא in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reading that 'ולמען ילמדו' excludes a mute because one who cannot speak cannot learn
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real-life case of two mutes who appeared to follow the learning in רבי's בית מדרש suggests that mutes can learn, so 'ילמדו' should not exclude them.

steps.title: The mute relatives turn out to know all of the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The story ends: רבי prayed for the two mute men, they were healed, and it turned out they had learned הלכה, ספרא, ספרי and the whole תלמוד. So a mute person can learn.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי prayed for them and they were healed. It then turned out that they had learned הלכה, ספרא, ספרי, and the entire תלמוד!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story it started in Step 6. The ending shows that mute people can learn, which challenges the ברייתא from Step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said 'so they may learn' leaves out a mute person, as if he cannot learn. But these two men were mute and still learned everything. So 'cannot speak, so cannot learn' seems to be false.

keyTerms.meaning: Mercy. Here it means prayer asking for mercy.
They had learned and knew it well
Collections of teachings that explain the פסוקים of the תורה

phrases.english: And רבי prayed for mercy on them
and they were healed
and it was found that they had learned
הלכה, ספרא and ספרי
phrases.notes: Here 'הלכה' means the משנה. ספרא explains ויקרא, and ספרי explains במדבר and דברים.

phrases.english: and the entire תלמוד!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story that Step 6 began, which completes the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reading in Step 5 that 'so they may learn' leaves out someone who cannot speak.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These men were mute, yet they had learned הלכה, ספרא, ספרי and the entire תלמוד. So being unable to speak does not stop a person from learning.

steps.title: Read the word as 'so they may teach'
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא answers that the פסוק should be read 'יְלַמְּדוּ', meaning 'so they may teach.' A mute person may be able to learn, but he cannot teach others.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: Read the word as 'so that they may teach.'
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא answers the challenge. He reads the same letters with different vowels, so the word means 'teach' instead of 'learn.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that mute people can learn. מר זוטרא agrees with that. He says the exemption is because a mute person cannot teach out loud. So the ברייתא's ruling stays the same, but the reason changes.

keyTerms.meaning: Read it as. Read the same letters with different vowels.

phrases.english: מר זוטרא said:
Read it as 'so that they may teach.'
phrases.notes: The letters stay the same. Only the vowels change, so 'learn' (יִלְמְדוּ) becomes 'teach' (יְלַמְּדוּ).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the story in Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'So they may learn' leaves out a mute person because he cannot learn.
steps.terutzMaskana: A mute person is left out because he cannot teach others, even though he can learn.

steps.title: Proof that the real meaning is 'teach'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the meaning is certainly 'so they may teach.' If the point were only that a mute person cannot learn, the phrase 'so they may hear' would already cover that. So the second phrase must be adding something new.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It is certainly 'so they may teach.' Suppose you thought it means 'so they may learn,' with the reason being that someone who cannot speak cannot learn, just as someone who cannot hear cannot learn. Then that would already come from 'so they may hear'! So it must certainly be 'so they may teach.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי goes further than מר זוטרא. He proves that 'teach' is the true meaning of the פסוק, not just a creative re-reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'so they may hear' leaves out the deaf because they cannot learn, then the rule 'whoever cannot learn is exempt' is already taught there. The phrase about learning would then add nothing. It must therefore teach a new reason: someone who cannot teach is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: If it would enter your mind. Used to set up an idea the גמרא will reject.

steps.whatToRemember: A mute person is exempt from הקהל because he cannot teach, not because he cannot learn. Through the גזירה שוה, this exemption also applies to ראיה.
steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי's point is not just that mute people can learn. It is that the 'learn' reading would make the phrase repeat what 'so they may hear' already teaches.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
It certainly is 'so that they may teach,'
for if it would enter your mind that it means 'so that they may learn,'
and since he does not speak, he does not learn,
and since he does not hear, he does not learn,
then this already comes from 'so that they may hear'!
Rather, it certainly is 'so that they may teach.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports מר זוטרא and goes further. He proves the 'teach' reading is the actual meaning of the פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That the פסוק means 'so they may teach'
steps.raayaSupportSource: If it meant 'learn,' it would repeat what 'so they may hear' already teaches.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A mute person is exempt from הקהל because he cannot teach.

steps.title: Someone deaf in one ear is exempt from ראיה
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום rules that a person deaf in even one ear is exempt from ראיה, because the פסוק about הקהל says 'in their ears,' which means both ears.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי תנחום said: Someone who is deaf in one ear is exempt from ראיה, as it says 'in their ears.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי תנחום about a person who can hear with only one ear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about הקהל says 'in their ears,' so הקהל requires hearing with both ears. Because ראיה is learned from הקהל through the גזירה שוה (Step 3), the same exemption applies to ראיה.
steps.whatToRemember: Whoever is exempt from הקהל, even someone deaf in only one ear, is also exempt from ראיה.

phrases.english: רבי תנחום said:
One who is deaf in one ear
is exempt from ראיה,
as it is stated: 'in their ears.'
phrases.notes: דברים 31:11, the פסוק about הקהל. It connects to ראיה through the גזירה שוה from Step 3.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining why deaf and mute people are exempt, the גמרא adds a further case: someone deaf in just one ear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person deaf in one ear is exempt from ראיה, learned from 'in their ears' in the הקהל פסוק.

steps.title: Isn't 'In Their Ears' Needed for All of Israel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי תנחום: the word 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is needed to teach that the reading at הקהל must reach all of Israel, so it is not free to teach about one ear.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this word 'in their ears' is needed to teach 'in the ears' of all of Israel!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי תנחום's source. It says the word 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' already has a different job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word in the תורה that is busy teaching one lesson usually can't also be used for a second lesson. If 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' teaches that the reading must be heard by the whole nation, it can't also teach that a person needs two working ears.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for (a different lesson)

phrases.english: But this word, "in their ears"
is needed for something else:
"in the ears" of all of Israel!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source רבי תנחום used in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי תנחום's use of 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' to exempt one who is deaf in one ear
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word is already used to teach that the reading must reach all of Israel, so it is not free for a new lesson.

steps.title: That Comes From 'Before All Israel'
steps.stepSummary: The lesson that the reading must reach all of Israel comes from the phrase 'נֶגֶד כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: That lesson is learned from 'before all Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a different phrase teaches that the whole nation must hear. That leaves 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' free for רבי תנחום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'before all Israel' already say the reading is meant for the entire nation. So 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' isn't needed for that lesson.

phrases.english: That lesson is learned from "before all Israel."
phrases.notes: דברים 31:11

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the competing lesson to a different phrase
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is needed to teach that all of Israel must hear.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'נֶגֶד כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל' teaches that, so 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is free.

steps.title: 'Before All Israel' Alone Wouldn't Require Hearing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that 'before all Israel' alone might mean the people only need to be present, even if they can't hear. So 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is needed to teach that they must actually hear.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we only had 'before all Israel,' I would have thought it counts even if they don't hear. So the תורה wrote 'in their ears,' which means only when they hear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer again. 'Before all Israel' only tells us that the people must be there, not that they must be able to hear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' has a new job: teaching that the people must actually hear the reading, not just stand in front of it. Once again, it seems the word is not free for רבי תנחום's lesson about one ear.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (a mistaken first idea)

phrases.english: If we learned it only from "before all Israel,"
I would have said
that it counts even though they do not hear.
So the Merciful One wrote "in their ears,"
meaning: only when they actually hear.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מִ״נֶּגֶד כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answer in step 12 does not fully free up 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 12 that 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is not needed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Before all Israel' only requires being present, so 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is still needed to require actual hearing.

steps.title: Hearing Comes From 'So That They May Hear'
steps.stepSummary: The rule that the people must actually hear comes from 'לְמַעַן יִשְׁמְעוּ'. So 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is free to teach that one needs both ears.
steps.simpleTranslation: That lesson is learned from 'so that they may hear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a third phrase teaches that the people must actually hear. Now 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' really is free, and רבי תנחום's source stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every other job for 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' has been given to another phrase. So the word itself teaches the extra detail of 'ears', meaning both ears. A person deaf in one ear is therefore exempt.
steps.whatToRemember: Each lesson has its own phrase. 'Before all Israel' means the whole nation, 'so that they may hear' means they must actually hear, and 'in their ears' means both ears. That is why one who is deaf in one ear is exempt.

phrases.english: That lesson is learned from "so that they may hear."
phrases.notes: דברים 31:12, the same פסוק discussed back in step 9.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 13 and settles רבי תנחום's source.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the competing lesson to a different phrase
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' is needed to require actual hearing.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'לְמַעַן יִשְׁמְעוּ' requires hearing, so 'בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם' teaches that both ears are needed.

steps.title: One Lame in One Leg Is Exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום rules that a person lame in even one leg is exempt from ראיה, based on the word 'רְגָלִים', which sounds like 'legs'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי תנחום said: A person lame in one leg is exempt from appearing, as it says 'רְגָלִים'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי תנחום gives a second ruling that follows the same pattern as his ruling about ears. Someone who cannot walk on both legs is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'רְגָלִים', which means festival times, sounds like 'רַגְלַיִם', legs. This hints that going up to the בית המקדש requires two working legs.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt from appearing at the בית המקדש

phrases.english: Rabbi Tanchum said:
One who is lame in one leg
is exempt from appearing,
as it says: "times [regalim]."
phrases.notes: שמות 23:14. The word means festival times, but it sounds like "legs."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם: חִיגֵּר בְּרַגְלוֹ אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling by רבי תנחום, parallel to his ruling about one ear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who is lame in one leg is exempt from ראיה, learned from 'רְגָלִים'.

steps.title: Isn't 'רגלים' Needed for Artificial Legs?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that 'רְגָלִים' is needed to exclude people with artificial legs, so it is not free for רבי תנחום's lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: But 'רְגָלִים' is needed to exclude people with artificial legs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי תנחום's second source the same way it challenged the first. The word already has another job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People with artificial legs can walk, but they are exempt because they do not have real legs. If 'רְגָלִים' teaches that, it seems it cannot also teach about someone lame in one leg.

phrases.english: But "regalim" is needed
to exclude people with artificial legs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source רבי תנחום used in step 15.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word is already used to exclude people with artificial legs.

steps.title: Artificial Legs Are Excluded From 'פעמים'
steps.stepSummary: The exclusion of people with artificial legs comes from the word 'פְּעָמִים', which leaves 'רְגָלִים' free for רבי תנחום.
steps.simpleTranslation: That lesson is learned from 'פְּעָמִים'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a different word in a nearby פסוק teaches the law about artificial legs. Next it will prove that this word can mean feet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'פְּעָמִים' means 'times', but it can also mean feet. So it can teach that a person needs real feet, and 'רְגָלִים' stays free to require two working legs.

keyTerms.meaning: Times; can also mean feet or steps

phrases.english: That lesson is learned from "times [pe'amim],"
phrases.notes: שמות 23:17

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the competing lesson to a different word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'רְגָלִים' is needed to exclude people with artificial legs.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'פְּעָמִים' excludes them, so 'רְגָלִים' is free for one who is lame in one leg.

steps.title: Proof That 'פעמים' Means Feet
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא proves that 'פְּעָמִים' means feet, citing פסוקים from ישעיהו and שיר השירים.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'פְּעָמִים' means only feet. So it says: 'A foot shall trample it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.' And it says: 'How beautiful are your feet in sandals, daughter of the prince.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports its answer with a ברייתא. Two פסוקים show that the word 'פְּעָמִים' is used for feet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ישעיהו, 'פַּעֲמֵי דַלִּים' appears right next to 'רַגְלֵי עָנִי', so it clearly means feet. In שיר השירים, 'פְעָמַיִךְ' wear sandals, which only feet do. This proves that 'פְּעָמִים' can teach a law about real feet.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says (bringing a פסוק as support)

steps.whatToRemember: Two words teach two laws. 'פְּעָמִים' (feet) excludes people with artificial legs, and 'רְגָלִים' (legs) excludes one who is lame in even one leg.

phrases.english: as it was taught in a ברייתא: "pe'amim":
"pe'amim" means nothing other than feet.
And so it says:
"A foot shall trample it,
the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 26:6

phrases.english: And it says: "How beautiful are your feet
in sandals, daughter of the prince."
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 7:2

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 17 by showing that 'פְּעָמִים' means feet.
steps.raayaObject: That 'פְּעָמִים' means feet and can exclude people with artificial legs
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא citing ישעיהו 26:6 and שיר השירים 7:2

steps.title: רבא: The beautiful feet of Israel going up for the festival
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains 'מה יפו פעמיך' as praise for the feet of ישראל when they go up to ירושלים for the רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא taught: What does the פסוק 'How beautiful are your feet in sandals, daughter of the prince' mean? How pleasant are the feet of ישראל when they go up for the festival.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the last step used 'פְּעָמִים' to mean feet, the גמרא brings a teaching by רבא on the same פסוק. He reads a פסוק in שיר השירים as praising people who go up for the רגל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'פְעָמַיִךְ' means feet, just as the ברייתא in Step 18 showed. רבא connects it to עלייה לרגל, the מצוה our sugya is about. The pun works because רגל means both 'foot' and 'festival'.

keyTerms.meaning: Expounded; explained a פסוק in a deeper way
Going up to ירושלים for the festival

phrases.english: Rava expounded: What is that which is written:
"How beautiful are your feet in sandals,
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 7:2

phrases.english: daughter of the prince"
How pleasant are the feet of Israel
at the time they go up for the festival.
phrases.notes: Notice the wordplay: רגל means both 'foot' and 'festival'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the proof that פעמים means feet and brings an אגדה using that same word.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'מה יפו פעמיך' praises the feet of ישראל going up for the רגל.

steps.title: "Daughter of the prince" means the daughter of אברהם
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that 'בת נדיב' refers to ישראל as the daughter of אברהם, who is called a נדיב, and brings a פסוק from תהלים as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Daughter of the prince' means the daughter of אברהם אבינו, who is called a prince. As it says: 'The princes of the peoples gathered, the people of the God of אברהם.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא now explains the second half of the פסוק, 'בת נדיב'. He says the נדיב is אברהם and proves it from a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק from תהלים, the 'princes of the peoples' are tied to 'the God of אברהם'. That link shows that אברהם is the one called נדיב. This sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Prince; also a generous, noble person

phrases.english: "Daughter of the prince":
the daughter of Avraham our father
who is called a prince,
as it is said:
"The princes of the peoples gathered,
phrases.notes: תהלים 47:10

phrases.english: the people of the God of Avraham."

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּת נָדִיב — בִּתּוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's explanation with the second half of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'בת נדיב' refers to ישראל as the daughter of אברהם, who is called נדיב.

steps.title: Why only "the God of אברהם"?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק in תהלים mentions only 'the God of אברהם' and leaves out יצחק and יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The God of אברהם' — and not the God of יצחק and יעקב?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the proof-פסוק. Why would it name only אברהם?
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ is the God of all three אבות, so naming only אברהם looks strange. The question pushes us to find something special about אברהם that fits the word 'נדיבים'.

phrases.english: "The God of Avraham" —
and not the God of Yitzchak and Yaakov?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם, וְלֹא אֱלֹהֵי יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the פסוק just cited as proof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ה׳ is the God of all the אבות, so why does the פסוק single out אברהם?

steps.title: אברהם was the first of the converts
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק names אברהם because he was the first גר. The converts who follow him are the 'princes of the peoples'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it says 'the God of אברהם' because he was the first of the converts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אברהם is mentioned alone because he was the very first convert.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People from the nations who come close to ה׳ are called 'נדיבי עמים'. They gather to the God of אברהם because he started that path. That is why אברהם alone is called the נדיב.
steps.whatToRemember: ישראל going up for the רגל are praised as the 'daughter of the נדיב', meaning the children of אברהם, the first convert.

phrases.english: Rather: "The God of Avraham" —
because he was the first of the converts.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם — שֶׁהָיָה תְּחִילָּה לְגֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about why only אברהם is named.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a unique quality that fits the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Naming only אברהם seems to leave out יצחק and יעקב for no reason.
steps.terutzMaskana: אברהם is named because he was the first convert, the leader of the 'נדיבי עמים'.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק say the empty pit had no water?
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רבי תנחום, the גמרא asks why the פסוק about יוסף's pit says 'it had no water' when it already said 'the pit was empty'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: רב נתן בר מניומי taught in the name of רבי תנחום: What does 'And the pit was empty, there was no water in it' mean? Once it says 'the pit was empty', don't I already know there was no water in it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי תנחום, the same Sage from Step 15. It starts by pointing out that the פסוק seems to say the same thing twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Empty' already tells us there was no water. So the extra words 'אין בו מים' must be teaching something new. This question sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: From the implication of; from what is already understood

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
Rav Natan bar Minyomi expounded
in the name of Rabbi Tanchum:
What is that which is written:
"And the pit was empty, there was no water in it"?
phrases.notes: בראשית 37:24, the pit יוסף's brothers threw him into.

phrases.english: From the implication of what is said, "And the pit was empty,"
don't I know that there was no water in it?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִמַּשְׁמַע שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְהַבּוֹר רֵק — אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מָיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another, unrelated teaching of רבי תנחום, whose ruling appeared earlier.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do the seemingly extra words 'אין בו מים' teach?

steps.title: No water, but snakes and scorpions
steps.stepSummary: The extra words teach that the pit had no water but did have snakes and scorpions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: water it did not have, but snakes and scorpions it did have.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'no water' tells us only water was missing. Dangerous creatures were there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Empty' alone would mean nothing at all was inside. The words 'אין בו מים' narrow it down: water was missing, but other things were there. Those things were snakes and scorpions.

phrases.english: Rather: water there was not in it,
but snakes and scorpions there were in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: מַיִם אֵין בּוֹ, אֲבָל נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים יֵשׁ בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the double wording.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The pit lacked water but had snakes and scorpions.

steps.title: רבי יהושע asks his visitors what was new in the study hall
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how two students visited רבי יהושע in פקיעין, and he asked them what חידוש was taught in the בית המדרש that day.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה and רבי אלעזר בן חסמא went to greet רבי יהושע in פקיעין. He asked them: What new idea was taught in the study hall today?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story from a ברייתא. רבי יהושע asks his visiting students what new תורה was taught that day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story will lead to a דרשה about הקהל, the same מצוה the sugya discussed before. The question about a חידוש starts a short back-and-forth.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
There was an incident with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
and Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word בן; the square brackets add it back, so his full name is רבי אלעזר בן חסמא.

phrases.english: who went to greet Rabbi Yehoshua
in Peki'in.
He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: מָה חִידּוּשׁ הָיָה בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הַיּוֹם?
phrases.english: What new idea was there in the study hall today?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא story that will connect back to הקהל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opens the story: רבי יהושע asks what חידוש was taught.

steps.title: The students humbly hold back
steps.stepSummary: The students answer that they are his students and all their תורה comes from him, so what could they tell him that is new?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: We are your students, and we drink your water.
steps.whatsHappening: The students politely avoid answering. They say they could not teach their own רבי anything new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תורה is compared to water. They mean that everything they know they learned from him, so anything they say he must already know.

keyTerms.meaning: We drink your water (we learn all our Torah from you)

phrases.english: They said to him: We are your students
and we drink your water.
phrases.notes: Water here means Torah: everything we know, we learned from you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The students answer רבי יהושע's question by holding back.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They say they have nothing new to teach their own רבי.

steps.title: There is always something new in the study hall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע insists that a בית המדרש never goes a day without a חידוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Even so, a study hall cannot be without something new.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע does not accept their modesty. He insists that something new is always taught, so they should tell him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their humility does not change the fact that every day of learning brings something new. This pushes the conversation forward toward the actual דרשה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן,
phrases.english: He said to them: Even so,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ בְּלֹא חִידּוּשׁ.
phrases.english: it is impossible for a study hall to be without something new.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ בְּלֹא חִידּוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets aside the students' humble refusal.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is always a חידוש in the בית המדרש, so they must share it.

steps.title: Whose turn was it to lecture?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks who gave the lecture that week, and they answer רבי אלעזר בן עזריה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose שבת was it? It was the שבת of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע starts asking for details, beginning with who gave the lecture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lecturers took turns week by week. Learning that it was רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's turn tells us whose דרשה we are about to hear.

phrases.english: Whose Shabbos was it?
phrases.notes: He means: whose turn was it to give the lecture this week?

phrases.aramaic: שַׁבָּת שֶׁל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה הָיְתָה.
phrases.english: It was the Shabbos of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יהושע moves from asking in general to asking for specifics.

steps.title: The lecture was about הקהל — what did he teach?
steps.stepSummary: The students say the lecture was on פרשת הקהל, and רבי יהושע asks what דרשה was given on it. This sets up the next step.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what was the lecture about today? They said to him: About the section of הקהל. And what did he expound in it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע learns the topic was הקהל and asks what exactly was taught. This is a setup line: the actual דרשה comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story now connects back to the earlier part of the sugya about הקהל and the פסוקים 'באזניהם' and 'למען ישמעו'. The question 'ומה דרש בה' prepares for רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: The section about gathering all ישראל to hear the Torah

phrases.english: And about what was the lecture today?
They said to him: About the section of Hakhel.
And what did he expound in it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the questioning and narrows it to the topic and content of the lecture.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What was the topic, and what דרשה was given on it?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The topic was פרשת הקהל. The content of the דרשה comes in step 30.

steps.title: The דרשה on why little children come to הקהל
steps.stepSummary: The students report רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's דרשה: men come to learn, women come to hear, and small children come so that those who bring them receive שכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones.' If the men come to learn and the women come to hear, why do the little ones come? To give reward to those who bring them.
steps.whatsHappening: The students answer רבי יהושע's question from step 29 by telling him the דרשה that was said on פרשת הקהל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The דרשה notices that the פסוק lists three groups and asks what each group gains. Men and women each have a clear purpose, but small children cannot understand anything. So their coming must be for someone else: the parents earn שכר for bringing them.

keyTerms.meaning: Assemble; the gathering of all Jews in the בית המקדש after שמיטה to hear the Torah read
To hear (to listen, even without full understanding)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the famous source for the idea that bringing children to a holy gathering is itself a מצוה that earns reward, even if the children understand nothing.

phrases.english: "Assemble the people,
phrases.notes: דברים 31:12

phrases.english: the men and the women and the little ones."
If the men come to learn,
and the women come to hear,
why do the little ones come?
In order to give reward to those who bring them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַקְהֵל אֶת הָעָם הָאֲנָשִׁים וְהַנָּשִׁים וְהַטַּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יהושע's request in step 29 to hear the דרשה on הקהל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Inside the דרשה: why are little children included in הקהל?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So that those who bring them receive reward.

steps.title: רבי יהושע calls the teaching a good pearl
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע praises the דרשה and gently scolds the students for almost not telling him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: You had a good pearl in your hands, and you wanted to keep it from me?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע reacts to the דרשה with great excitement and praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This proves the point he made in step 27, that a בית המדרש never goes a day without a חידוש. The students had said they had nothing new to tell him. Now he shows them that they really did have something precious.

keyTerms.meaning: A good pearl; a precious idea
To make it lost; to keep it hidden

steps.whatToRemember: Even a teacher learns new things from what his students bring back. A single fresh insight in תורה is called a 'pearl.'

phrases.english: He said to them:
A good pearl was in your hands,
and you wanted to make it lost from me?
phrases.notes: He means: you almost kept this beautiful idea from me by saying you had nothing new.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the דרשה just told, and proves רבי יהושע's claim from step 27.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The students did have a חידוש: a precious one.

steps.title: A second דרשה on two פסוקים of affirming
steps.stepSummary: The students add that רבי אלעזר בן עזריה also expounded the פסוקים 'You affirmed ה׳ today' and 'ה׳ affirmed you today.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And he also expounded: 'You have affirmed ה׳ today' and 'ה׳ has affirmed you today.'
steps.whatsHappening: The students bring a second teaching from the same lecture. Here they only quote the two פסוקים, and this sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים use the same unusual word, הֶאֱמִיר, once for ישראל toward ה׳ and once for ה׳ toward ישראל. That matching language hints at a two-way relationship, which the next step will explain.

keyTerms.meaning: You have affirmed / declared as special
He has affirmed you / declared you special

phrases.english: And he further expounded:
"You have affirmed ה׳ today,"
phrases.notes: דברים 26:17

phrases.english: "And ה׳ has affirmed you today,"
phrases.notes: דברים 26:18

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two matching פסוקים about 'affirming' are the basis for a new דרשה.

steps.title: Each side makes the other one of a kind
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא tells ישראל: you made Me a unique entity in the world, so I will make you a unique entity in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to ישראל: You made Me one unique entity in the world, and I will make you one unique entity in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: This explains the two פסוקים from step 32. Each side 'affirms' the other by making it one-of-a-kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הֶאֱמִיר is understood to mean 'made into a חטיבה אחת,' something singled out and unique. ישראל does this for ה׳ by declaring Him the only God. ה׳ answers measure for measure by making ישראל a unique nation.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He
A single unique entity; something singled out and special

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning of the two פסוקים quoted in step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The relationship is two-way: ישראל makes ה׳ unique, and ה׳ makes ישראל unique.

steps.title: Proof from שמע ישראל, and the second proof begins
steps.stepSummary: The proof that ישראל makes ה׳ unique is שמע ישראל. Then the גמרא starts bringing a פסוק to prove that ה׳ makes ישראל unique.
steps.simpleTranslation: You made Me one unique entity in the world, as it is written: 'Hear, Israel, ה׳ is our God, ה׳ is One.' And I will make you one unique entity in the world, as it says:
steps.whatsHappening: Now each half of the idea gets a source. The first half is proven from שמע ישראל, and the proof for the second half comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When ישראל says 'ה׳ is One,' they declare Him unique, so this proves the first half. The words 'as it says' open the proof for the second half, but the פסוק itself only comes on the next amud.
